title: European audiences versus American audiences
summary: Greer says Europeans were more enthusiastic and tells of 300 girls singing Happy Birthday.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Did you see any difference between European audiences and American audiences?

Yeah. They were -- it's hard to say, but they were more enthusiastic for the simple reason -- it wasn't like in America, like you can go hear anybody you want. It was a rarity, and they were so overjoyed to see us in person and hear them in person that they were more enthusiastic.
Did the European women chase after musicians as much as they do in America?
Did the women over there chase
after musicians as much as they chase after musicians in America.
I mean, a lot of times musicians if they're popular, they're very popular with the women.
Well, at that time, we were always invited -- they were always giving up something for us, because when they like you, that was their way of showing their appreciation. Was over-enthusiastic.

I recall one time in Sweden on Duke's birthday, we were playing up there and 300 little girls, young teenagers they sang "Happy Birthday" in Swedish and walked down with flowers, and it happened to be on his birthday we were playing a concert, and during intermission they and another band played "Happy Birthday" and they all sang it in Swedish and all of them had a bouquet of flowers, right to the stage. You can imagine 300 bouquets of flowers and everybody singing, "Happy Birthday," yeah.
So you all were very well known in Europe, even before you got there, then?

We were the biggest thing since Barnum & Bailey. I tell you, they had on -- they call them buses here, they call them trams here, all on the side, like you see the bus, advertising on the side. The buses in New York, that's how it was.
